data.title: Trump: DOJ working to overturn Newsom's death row commutations
data.description:
President Trump slammed California Gov. Gavin Newsom Monday over the Democratic governor’s move to commute the death penalty for California death row inmates.

The president, speaking from the Justice Department, called Newsom’s actions “one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen.”

He said officials in the room “are working as hard as they can to get this travesty overturned in some form.”

He was joined by Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, among others. Some family members of victims also attended and gave remarks criticizing Newsom’s move.

“Newsom, a terrible governor in so many other ways, came along and stole away the only closure those families might ever have,” Trump said. “He stood with the murderers and the child slayers, but today we say the American people stand with you.”

Newsom commuted the sentences of 548 inmates, changing it instead to life in prison without parole. The governor in 2019 instituted a moratorium on the death penalty after taking office.

Trump said at the event that Newsom and the “radical left look at these heinous acts and their sympathy is not for the children of their parents, but for the monsters who extinguished innocent young lives.”

“Don’t understand it,” he said. “Never did.”

The governor is set to leave office in January.  This move is seen as a way for Newsom to platform himself ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign season.

In a letter to Californians earlier this month, he shared his decision saying he firmly believes “that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.”

“I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency,” he wrote.

In his letter he noted that the inmates inflicted “indescribable suffering” on those affected but said they he prays “hat this action will finally separate the memories of the victims of these crimes from the fate of those who harmed them.”

“We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims,” he wrote.

California has not executed anyone since 2006.

In a video released Monday, Newsom accused Trump of using presidential pardons for his friends, while prosecuting his enemies.

“America needs foundational federal reform. No president should turn the power of mercy into a business,” Newsom wrote in an X post with the video. “No one should be able to sell a pardon. Justice is not for sale.”

At the event, Trump announced he was donating $5,000 to the Trump accounts of the granddaughter of one of the victims whose killer Newsom commuted. He also said the Justice Department will award nearly $150 million to public safety grants.

Trump said that Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) will introduce legislation to strengthen the penalty in America called the Just Punishment for Murder Act. He signed the order in January to restore the death penalty.

data.title: Appeals court declines to halt Iowa lead detonation as Sand says feds should make call
data.description:
The Army’s plan to detonate tons of explosive lead material in Iowa is in limbo on Monday after Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) passed the decision back to President Trump and a federal appeals court declined to intervene.

Trump earlier in the day said that while he personally supported detonating the lead-containing munitions, he would leave it up to the governor and the courts. It’s not immediately clear whether the detonations will now move forward on Wednesday as previously scheduled.

In a post on X, Sand said the administration “should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks.”

Sand also reiterated his call for the administration to release more information to the public about the detonation.

“Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” Sand wrote.  

“That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I’ve asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible,” he added. 

At the same time, a three-judge panel for the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to halt the detonation, denying an emergency request from the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club to block an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) permit that authorized the activity while its broader legal challenge continues. 

The environmental groups argue that the EPA unlawfully bypassed environmental regulations in approving the permit and did not give the public enough notice of the plan, which they said could expose thousands of families in surrounding communities to elevated levels of toxic dust. 

“We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide,” the judges wrote in an unsigned opinion. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House, the Army and Earthjustice, which represents the environmental groups, for comment. 

Trump had said earlier he would only allow the detonations, which had been slated for Wednesday, to move forward with approval from Sand and the courts. 

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump wrote on social media.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” he added.

The Army announced earlier this month that it planned to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, saying it was the safest way to eliminate what it described as an “explosive safety hazard.”

It noted that the detonation could cause a plume that contains lead, a toxic metal that is particularly harmful to babies and children.

Exposure to it can cause damage to the brain and nervous system, lower IQ and learning and behavioral problems in children. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the EPA.

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

data.title: Jensen Huang's dramatic return to Nvidia: Five takeaways
data.description:
Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday morning in one of the most shocking developments seen on Wall Street in years.

Huang, the chip behemoth’s co-founder, had been ousted by Nvidia’s board amid an admitted affair with a woman alleged to be working with Chinese intelligence, Alice Huang.

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, has not commented since the matter became public while the Chinese government has decried the charge as a smear.

Jensen Huang, who is married, is also reported to have had a second affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12, causing the company’s share price to slide, and nerves to fray around artificial intelligence (AI) more generally.

The Nvidia board had ruled out reinstating Huang before executing a startling U-turn.

Here are five takeaways.

Trump, for good or bad, was the decisive factor

President Trump is making no bones about the fact that he was the decisive factor in getting Huang reinstated. Whether that is a good or bad thing is in the eye of the beholder.

“I believe my intervention was very important,” the president told CNBC in a telephone interview, in which he also said, “The board decided to do what we wanted them to do.”

In a social media post, Trump praised the board for having made “the correct and proper decision.”

Trump’s defenders contend he acted to resurrect a key figure who can keep the United States ahead of China in the AI ‘arms race.’

But there’s a very different interpretation: That Trump has ridden roughshod over major security concerns regarding Jensen Huang’s dealings with Alice Huang – in part because taking those concerns seriously would risk further declines on Wall Street.

Over the weekend, The New York Times reported that Alice Huang had maintained contact with an official in China’s top spy agency from spring 2025 until this fall — and that a man often identified as her husband had worked with the same agency, the Ministry of State Security.

In his social media post, Trump contended that Attorney General Todd Blanche had “confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Jensen Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

But the narrow and legalistic framing leaves obvious questions unanswered, including what would happen if such evidence were to come to light – and whether Huang enjoys impunity for inappropriate conduct because of his closeness to Trump.

Several Republicans join chorus of criticism

For once, a divisive issue did not break along entirely partisan lines in Washington.

Several Republicans expressed unease about Huang’s reinstatement.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) noted on social media that the Nvidia board had previously suggested Huang had lacked “candor” in his dealings with them. “His behavior does not support reinstatement,” the GOP senator wrote.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) expressed concern about the “national security risk” of the reinstatement, adding in reference to Alice Huang, “The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough not to rehire [Jensen] Huang.”

Neither Ricketts nor Cramer are so readily inclined to criticize Trump as two others who also expressed worry about the move, Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and John Curtis (R-Utah).

Even former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), usually a reliable supporter of Trump, weighed in, asserting that “Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions.”

Democrats rage – and ready investigations

Trump’s central role in Huang’s reinstatement is fueling Democratic desire to dig into the matter, especially once they take the majority in the Senate and the House in January.

Soon-to-be-Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said the decision taken by the Nvidia board was “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” Jeffries promised a “swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by Nvidia” and suggested his party would place a particular spotlight on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Jeffries additionally asserted: “We will not allow America’s national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain.”

Jeffries’ counterpart in the Senate, Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.), for his part pledged that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), frequently to the fore in pressing for scrutiny of major corporations, called the decision to bring Huang back “reckless.” Warren wrote on social media that the Trump administration “needs to explain what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement.”

Meanwhile, 2016 Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton suggested in a social media post that Huang’s return amounted to a scandal on several different fronts.

Clinton, jabbing at Trump’s preference to refer to artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence,” suggested the Huang matter should be dubbed “Supergate.”

Nvidia soared – and so did the markets

The news of Huang’s return broke before U.S. equity markets opened on Monday – and the results were explosive.

Nvidia soared more than 31 percent for the day. Its advance added almost $1 trillion to its valuation – an extraordinary one-day gain reflecting investor faith in Huang. It also means enormous gains for the CEO himself. Forbes projected that Huang’s net worth increased $33 billion for the day.

The broader market also benefited, rebounding with enormous force from Friday’s tech rout. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 6.5 percent while the broader-based S&P 500 went up 4.7 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 3 percent.

There are, of course, questions about whether those gains will be sustained. Many financial experts have concerns about how central AI has become to the broader market.

In addition, Nvidia is still well below its all-time peak. The stock closed on Monday at roughly $165 per share. Its high point, less than two months ago, was about $243.

All of that being said, Monday’s massive rally will have buoyed spirits on Wall Street and among Americans whose retirement plans rest heavily on the stock market’s fortunes.

Bigger questions about billionaire misbehavior

Amid all the political back-and-forth, there are other issues raised by Huang’s reinstatement.

Even setting aside the national security implications of his affair with the alleged Chinese spy, is his earlier lack of candor no longer a problem? What about the reported affair with the Nvidia executive?

To some, the whole farrago all raises serious questions about whether CEOs can become too big – or too well-connected – to face accountability.

“Opponents of unfettered capitalism have a powerful new marketing tool,” Wall Street Journal columnist James Mackintosh wrote on Monday. “And he wears a leather jacket.”

data.title: Appeals court breathes new life into Trump's fight over hush money conviction
data.description:
An appeals panel handed President Trump a win on Monday in his fight to overturn his hush money criminal conviction in New York, ruling that a judge wrongly denied his effort to move the case into federal court. 

It marks Trump’s biggest legal victory yet in his efforts to transfer his case out of New York’s state courts, which his lawyers hope will provide an easier path to toss his 34-count felony conviction that stems from a 2016 hush money payment to an adult film actor. The fate of Trump’s appeal remains unclear. 

The president’s effort to move courts failed before. Trump’s latest attempt cites the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling, saying he has the legal right to bring it up before a federal judge as a defense, but the ruling didn’t land until after his trial. Despite the late timing, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit agreed that’s “good cause” for another try.

“We disagree with the district court. First, the district court erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case after a federal officer defendant has been convicted,” the 2nd Circuit wrote in its unsigned ruling. 

Monday’s decision effectively puts a halt to Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s state court system and moves it to federal court, where the president will continue pressing his arguments that the case should remain there. 

It breathes new life into Trump’s appeal of the jury’s verdict finding him guilty on all 34 counts of falsifying business records in connection with a $130,000 hush money payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels to conceal an alleged affair from voters during the 2016 presidential campaign.

Ultimately, the president’s lawyers hope the federal judiciary will agree the jury saw evidence protected by the Supreme Court’s immunity ruling and rule that the guilty verdict can’t stand — an argument Trump’s New York trial judge rejected.

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s (D) office declined to comment.

“President Trump appreciates the Second Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System,” a spokesman for Trump’s legal team said in a statement. 

“As today’s order highlights, the Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal Constitution, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed. President Trump will keep defeating the Liberal Hoaxes at every turn,” he added. 

Notably, the president’s legal team in the next phase won’t be facing the same federal trial judge who has rejected Trump’s arguments multiple times before. U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein died at the age of 92 last month. 

The case has not yet been reassigned.

data.title: Commerce Department adds Megaspeed to trade backlist amid Nvidia scandal
data.description:
The Commerce Department moved to add the company at the center of Nvidia’s national security scandal, Megaspeed, to its trade entity blacklist on Monday, according to federal records.

The move, published in the Federal Register on Monday, comes as scrutiny mounts on the Commerce Department to tighten its chip export controls following reports Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle Nvidia’s chips to China.

The allegations surfaced amid reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with onetime Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China.

According to the Federal Register, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) made the decision for Megaspeed and six entities after determining “significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.”

Semafor first reported the BIS designation Monday.

As details around Huang’s alleged affair unfolded earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the Trump administration’s failure to place Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, on the U.S. trade blacklist for national security concerns.

“Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent told CNBC this month. “But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly took a softer line on Nvidia over the tech giant’s AI chip sales to China and Axios reported Bessent confronted the Commerce chief earlier this month about the delay. Lutnick, according to Axios, told Bessent he would “look into it.”

The allegations of Huang’s affair with Alice Huang prompted his resignation as Nvidia’s CEO and president earlier this month, but the company’s Board of Directors took a sharp reversal and unanimously voted to reinstate him on Monday.

The Nvidia CEO is scheduled to appear for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 in front of three House committees — the Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence Committee and the Select Committee on China. Jensen Huang will then testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

Lutnick has also agreed to appear before Congress on the matter.

data.title: Key House Democrat will oppose permitting reform bill
data.description:
Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) on Monday said he will oppose a Senate-passed bill that seeks to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy and infrastructure.

Levin, a clean energy advocate, said in a statement that with the 2026 Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), “there’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment.”

“The bill would modernize a power grid that too often can’t carry affordable clean energy to the homes that need it, and it would require data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades instead of passing the cost on to families,” he said.

But he added that the bill raised concerns, including placing a limit on “California’s ability to protect its own water, weaken the science behind endangered species decisions, and keep courts from halting a project even when an agency skips the review the law requires.”

Levin also pointed to President Trump’s approvals for offshore leases and said BAAJA would make it “extremely hard” for future presidential administrations to overturn the law.

“For those of us who have spent years fighting to keep new oil rigs off the California coast, that’s a serious threat,” he said.

“Tribal nations have warned that the bill’s changes to historic preservation law could endanger sacred sites and undercut Tribal sovereignty, and they deserved a far bigger voice in writing it,” Levin continued. “Those harms would be permanent, while the clean energy gains would rise or fall with whoever happens to be carrying out the law.”

He said that the latest iteration of the bill would be “giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”

“There’s still time to get this right. If House and Senate leaders from both parties sit down together and negotiate sufficient changes, I’ll be ready to vote yes,” he said.

Levin represents California’s 49th Congressional District, which straddles between northern San Diego County and southern Orange County, encompassing the cities of Carlsbad, Dana Point, San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.

The Senate passed BAAJA 62-33 last Thursday, spearheaded by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) Sens. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) were the only Republicans to vote against the bill, while 15 Democrats voted in favor of the bill.

Other opponents of the bill say it would bolster fossil fuels and mining, loosen environmental laws and limit the ability of a project’s opponents to challenge it in court.

Supporters say it will build the U.S. economy and allow for upgrades to the country’s infrastructure, including energy, to commence faster. They also say it will help lower the nation’s planet-warming emissions.

Yet the bill faces a crowded lame-duck calendar, including a possible lapse in federal funding, with some Democratic lawmakers deliberating over how to respond to funds going toward the Iran war or risk a government shutdown.

data.title: Zacharia attacks California bar's board members over 'political' probe
data.description:
Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on Monday attacked the California State Bar Association’s board members for conducting a “political” probe in connection with a complaint alleging that she had never passed the bar exam while claiming she was an attorney.

“Listen, these people are not unbiased,” Zacharia told “Human Events” host and conservative podcast host Jack Posobiec. “This is a political operation. It’s a hit job, and I can most 100 percent assuredly say that there will be no issues at all, Jack.”

She criticized the state bar’s vice chair, Dr. Mark W. Toney, who she said “does not hold a Juris Doctor,” or a graduate-entry law degree, and was appointed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D). According to California’s judicial branch, however, the state’s Supreme Court designates the chair and vice chair.

“And then you have another woman who graduated from a law school that’s 154th [in the nation], and my law school is number 47, it’s Pepperdine, and –– Pepperdine Law,” she continued, referring to Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in Malibu.

It’s unclear who Zacharia is referring to, though attorney member Cynthia Grande received her Juris Doctor from the University of the Paciﬁc-McGeorge School of Law in Sacramento. U.S. News & World Report’s rankings for “Best Law Schools” hold the law school in 152nd.

Zacharia then said another board member gave “a lot of very distasteful commentary on President Trump and specifically with Johnny Eastman.” The California Supreme Court disbarred former lawyer John Eastman in April, years after he led efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election in Trump’s favor.

Zacharia also accused lawyer and journalist Judd Legum of being an “operative” for John Podesta, former President Clinton’s White House chief of staff and chair of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign.

“He was, I guess, maybe a law student for Podesta and he calls him a close friend,” Zacharia continued. “And he wrote the initial, long Substack discussing what he thought was a problem … He was one of the biggest operatives in amplifying the Russiagate narrative, the Russagate hoax.”

Legum reported on his Substack “Popular Information” last month that there was no evidence that Zacharia passed a bar exam or had been admitted to practice law in any state. She was not listed as a member of the State Bar of California, nor the State Bar of Texas or the D.C. Bar.

On Monday, he responded on to Zacharia’s remarks on the social platform X that while he was a student at Georgetown Law School, he was Podesta’s research assistant.

“After I graduated, I took the Maryland bar exam, passed, and was admitted to practice,” he added.

The original complaint filed to the California State Bar Association, filed by the nonprofit watchdog group Campaign for Accountability earlier this month, accused Zacharia of breaking the law and requested that it open an investigation.

Her spokesperson previously told the Los Angeles Times that the claims in the complaint were “baseless” and “politically motivated.”

California law prohibits anyone who is not licensed by the state bar from presenting themselves as a lawyer, and a conviction is a misdemeanor “punishable by up to one year in a county jail or by a fine of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment.”

Trump defended Zacharia on Saturday. He said in an interview with Fox News’s Kayleigh McEnany, another former Trump White House press secretary, that he saw “the way [Zacharia] was treated” and told her “you don’t need this.”

“She might have been able to fight her way out of it, but why should she be put in that position?” he said.

data.title: Northeast braces for 'bomb cyclone' during Thanksgiving travel
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A storm system that could bring heavy rain, strong winds and potential flooding will likely impact Thanksgiving travel for many in the Northeast, according to forecasters.

By Tuesday, daytime temps will struggle to rise above the 40s in New York City, followed by overnight temperatures near or below freezing across the area. The chill returns during the daytime Wednesday.

As of Monday morning, the heaviest rain is expected to arrive in the afternoon and evening on Thanksgiving.

The Macy’s Centennial Thanksgiving Day Parade will go on rain or shine. However, depending on wind strength, it could affect balloon flight for the parade.

Expect around 1 to 2 inches of rain; higher amounts are possible locally. Winds could gust up to 40 mph near the coast and possibly higher locally. Flooding and beach erosion are also possible. Breezy conditions will continue on Friday.

West Coast not spared

Rainy and windy weather was also expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

San Francisco is bracing for flooding along its waterfront areas through Thursday.

Airport crews were preparing by checking pump stations and keeping drainage areas clear, said Doug Yakel, a spokesperson for San Francisco International Airport.

The low-lying airport also has backup pumps, sandbags and portable flood barriers, he said.

Holiday travel by the numbers

Despite fewer Americans expected to hit the roads and skies for Thanksgiving travel this year, AAA estimates that 81.5 million people are expected to travel over 50 miles for the holiday.

NewsNation local affiliate WPIX in New York contributed to this report.

data.title: First new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer approved in decades
data.description:
(NewsNation) — The Food and Drug Administration approved a new treatment for early-stage, estrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, the first new hormone therapy for early-stage cancer in more than 20 years.

The FDA approved giredestrant, under the brand name Wilserdly, as a post-surgery treatment for adults with the most common subtype of breast cancer for patients with Stage 1, 2 or 3 disease.

Breast cancer is the second most common cancer among women in the U.S., and roughly 70% of breast cancers are hormone receptor-positive, which means estrogen fuels the growth of the cancer.

Traditionally, people with early-stage, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer are treated with surgery followed by endocrine therapy, including drugs like tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor. However, some patients struggle with the side effects of those drugs, and recurrence is still a concern.

Wilserdly has been approved for use alone after surgery and comes as a once-daily oral tablet. It belongs to a class of drugs known as oral estrogen receptor antagonists, which help block estrogen from binding to receptors on cancer cells and break down the receptors, helping to block tumor growth.

“For patients with early-stage hormone-driven breast cancer, the goal after surgery is to keep the cancer from coming back,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence. “Our review focused on whether Wilserdly could reduce that risk more effectively than the hormone therapies patients already receive. The evidence showed that it could, supporting today’s approval of a new option for patients at intermediate to high risk of recurrence.”

In a randomized trial, Wilserdly reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard hormone therapy. After three years, 92.4% of patients taking Wilserdly were alive and had no invasive breast cancer, compared to 89.6% of those receiving traditional hormone therapy.

Side effects of Wilserdly include muscle and joint pain, hot flashes, tiredness, headache, nausea, slower heart rate, dizziness, numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, increased liver enzymes, lower blood counts, high blood fat levels and changes in kidney test results.

Wilserdly can harm a developing fetus if taken during pregnancy, and women who have not completed menopause need additional hormone-suppressing medication. Men with breast cancer can also take Wilserdly.
